Even if the ultimate code change is in a matcher, this is a very plausible integration point.

behavior_items: The reproducer uses Fortran 2018 coarray team support via `iso_fortran_env%team_type`, declares a `team` variable, and invokes `form team (1, team)` to create or assign a team context before entering a named `CHANGE TEAM` block.

`team_construct_name: change team(team)` is a named construct header; inside it, `exit team_construct_name` relies on the compiler recognizing the construct name as a valid target for `EXIT` within a `CHANGE TEAM` region.

`end team team_construct_name` is the matching named terminator; the standard allows a construct name there, so the parser must accept the optional name and validate that it matches the opening construct.
Gfortran 8.2.0 rejects the construct header as `Unclassifiable statement`, which indicates the front end does not parse the `CHANGE TEAM` statement form with a leading construct name.

Because the construct name is not entered into the surrounding name/scope machinery, the later `EXIT team_construct_name` is diagnosed as `unknown`, even though it should resolve to the named `CHANGE TEAM` block.
The `END TEAM team_construct_name` line is also rejected as `Unclassifiable statement`, showing the same parser gap on the matching terminator syntax rather than a downstream semantic issue.
The `if (.true.)` condition makes the `EXIT` execute unconditionally, so the body is designed to test only the parser/control-flow handling of named team constructs, not runtime team semantics.

The intended successful path would skip `error stop 'fail'` and print `pass`, so the reproducer checks whether the compiler can parse and compile a conforming named `CHANGE TEAM` / `END TEAM` pair without falling into the error stop path.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: This reproducer exercises Fortran 2018 named `CHANGE TEAM` constructs: it opens a team region, gives it the construct name `team_construct_name`, exits that construct by name, and closes it with `END TEAM team_construct_name`. The bug in gfortran 8.2.0 is in front-end parsing and name resolution for the new syntax: the compiler fails to recognize the named `CHANGE TEAM` header and matching `END TEAM` terminator, so the construct name is never registered for `EXIT` resolution, causing spurious parse and unknown-name errors instead of accepting the standard-conforming code.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern points to a front-end parser/statement-classification gap for Fortran 2018 team constructs with optional construct names. The same named identifier is rejected at the opening `CHANGE TEAM`, then propagates into a bogus `EXIT`-target lookup failure, and the matching `END TEAM <name>` is rejected as well. That combination strongly suggests GCC 8.2.0 lacks grammar or AST support for named `CHANGE TEAM` / `END TEAM` forms, rather than an issue in the reproducer or in runtime coarray execution.
possible_causes: Fortran parser grammar in `gfortran` does not accept an optional construct name before `CHANGE TEAM`, so the statement is classified as unclassifiable instead of entering the coarray team construct parsing path.
The front end’s statement matcher for `END TEAM` is missing support for the optional construct name token sequence, causing the terminator to be rejected as invalid syntax.
The construct-name bookkeeping for named team blocks is not wired into the symbol/label resolution used by `EXIT`, so the named `CHANGE TEAM` region is never registered as a valid exit target.

Handling of new Fortran 2018 coarray control constructs may be incomplete in the `resolve.c` / parser-to-semantics handoff, with named team constructs omitted from the shared construct-stack logic used by other named blocks.

Lexer/token-sequence handling for `CHANGE TEAM` may be too rigid and only recognize the unnamed form, so the presence of a leading construct name prevents the parser from reducing the statement correctly.
evidence: `team_construct_name: change team(team)` is rejected immediately with `Error: Unclassifiable statement`, which indicates parse-level support is missing for the named form.
`exit team_construct_name` then reports `Name 'team_construct_name' in EXIT statement ... is unknown`, consistent with the construct name never being entered into scope metadata.
`end team team_construct_name` is also rejected as `Unclassifiable statement`, showing the same syntax handling gap at the closing statement.
The reproducer uses standard Fortran 2018 named team-construct syntax, so the failures align with compiler support missing for a conforming language feature.
The unconditional `if (.true.)` means control-flow semantics are not under test; the only observed failures are front-end recognition and name resolution errors.

selected_files.reason: Most likely location of the bug because the primary failure is parse-time: the named header `team_construct_name: change team(team)` and terminator `end team team_construct_name` are both rejected as `Unclassifiable statement`. That strongly points to missing statement classification or construct-name handling for Fortran 2018 `CHANGE TEAM`/`END TEAM` syntax in the main Fortran parser.

Highly suspicious because gfortran statement matchers typically implement detailed syntax recognition after initial classification. Support for optional construct names on `CHANGE TEAM` and `END TEAM` may be absent or incomplete here, especially for the new F2018 team-construct forms.

The `EXIT team_construct_name` error indicates the construct name was never registered as a valid enclosing construct. Even if parsing is the first failure, named construct bookkeeping and EXIT-target resolution for `CHANGE TEAM` may also be missing or incomplete in semantic resolution logic here.

If `CHANGE TEAM` named-construct support required parser state, statement enums, or construct-stack declarations, the corresponding parser interfaces or data structures may need updates here alongside `parse.cc`.

Possible companion file if matcher prototypes, enums, or shared matching interfaces for `CHANGE TEAM`/`END TEAM` syntax were not extended for the named form, especially since the bug appears tied to statement matching support.

Matches a member separator. With standard FORTRAN this is '%', but with DEC structures we must carefully match dot ('.'). Because operators are spelled ".op.", a dotted string such as "x.y.z..." can be either a component reference chain or a combination of binary operations. There is no real way to win because the string may be grammatically ambiguous. The following rules help avoid ambiguities - they match some behavior of other (older) compilers. If the rules here are changed the test cases should be updated. If the user has problems with these rules they probably deserve the consequences. Consider "x.y.z": (1) If any user defined operator ".y." exists, this is always y(x,z) (even if ".y." is the wrong type and/or x has a member y). (2) Otherwise if x has a member y, and y is itself a derived type, this is (x->y)->z, even if an intrinsic operator exists which can handle (x,z). (3) If x has no member y or (x->y) is not a derived type but ".y." is an intrinsic operator (such as ".eq."), this is y(x,z). (4) Lastly if there is no operator ".y." and x has no member "y", it is an error. It is worth noting that the logic here does not support mixed use of member accessors within a singl

Match a stop-code after an (ERROR) STOP or PAUSE statement. The requirements for a stop-code differ in the standards. Fortran 95 has R840 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] R841 stop-code is scalar-char-constant or digit [ digit [ digit [ digit [ digit ] ] ] ] Fortran 2003 matches Fortran 95 except R840 and R841 are now R849 and R850. Fortran 2008 has R855 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] R856 allstop-stmt is ALL STOP [ stop-code ] R857 stop-code is scalar-default-char-constant-expr or scalar-int-constant-expr Fortran 2018 has R1160 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] [ , QUIET = scalar-logical-expr] R1161 error-stop-stmt is ERROR STOP [ stop-code ] [ , QUIET = scalar-logical-expr] R1162 stop-code is scalar-default-char-expr or scalar-int-expr For free-form source code, all standards contain a statement of the form: A blank shall be used to separate names, constants, or labels from adjacent keywords, names, constants, or labels. A stop-code is not a name, constant, or label. So, under Fortran 95 and 2003, STOP123 is valid, but it is invalid Fortran 2008.
